comment: The taxpayer raised that allegation (¶18), but the court held that limited discussion of a reply does not, by itself, prove it was ignored. It left the adequacy of the order’s reasoning for appeal (¶19–20, ¶31). The hearing dates cited by NoticeCheck concern a separate notice of hearing issue (¶21–22).

The cited hearing dates say nothing about the order’s reasons (¶5). The court treated the adequacy of the order’s reasoning as a matter for appeal and made no finding that the order was non-speaking (¶19–20, ¶31).

The order records three hearing dates, but the taxpayer disputed receiving notice of them (¶5, ¶21). The court said service was a factual question for the appellate authority, so it did not determine whether the hearing requirement was met (¶22). Repeating the same excerpt three times adds no evidence.

The SCN proposed ₹5,51,34,232, and the judgment says the order confirmed that proposed tax demand (¶1, ¶5). It identifies no added demand or different grounds. The court made no section 75(7) finding.

It gives the financial years and the SCN and order dates (¶5), but does not assess the section 74 time limits. The court did not decide whether the SCN or order was timely. The limitation mentioned in ¶31 concerns a possible appeal, not the section 74 deadline.

The court lists the grounds of challenge in ¶2 and in judgment paragraphs 11 and 17 (both within the supplied ¶5). None concerns section 168A or a COVID extension notification. Judgment paragraphs 6 and 8 give the SCN and order dates, but do not establish NoticeCheck’s additional claim that extensions could not affect timeliness.

Answered for the narrow question of whether the SCN alleged conduct that could support section 74. It alleged mis-declaration, undervaluation and clandestine clearance (judgment paragraph 6, within supplied ¶5). That does not establish that the allegations were proved. The listed grounds of challenge do not include missing section 74 ingredients (judgment paragraphs 11 and 17, within supplied ¶5).

missed: The court found no defect warranting interference and dismissed the writ petition (judgment paragraphs 29–30, within supplied ¶5). It left the petitioner free to pursue an appeal (paragraph 31).

comment: The quoted order says the taxpayer requested adjournments and the officer declined them, citing lack of sufficient cause (¶2). The court did not find that refusal unlawful. It set aside the orders solely because they gave no meaningful reasons for rejecting the taxpayer’s reply (¶1, ¶3–6).
The officer dismissed the reply with the quoted stock phrase (¶2). The court held that the order was wholly unreasoned and set it aside on that ground (¶3–6).

The adjournment requests appear only in the officer’s order quoted at ¶2. The court identified the unreasoned rejection of the reply as the ground for setting the orders aside (¶1, ¶3–6). These excerpts do not support a second procedural defect.

The petitioner challenged Notification No. 56/2023-CT, which NoticeCheck identifies as relevant to the time limit (¶1). The officer’s order also refers to an approaching 31 August 2024 deadline (¶2). It set aside the orders for lack of reasons and expressly kept the notification challenge open (¶5–7). The judgment does not itself establish NoticeCheck’s claim that the order was timely only because of the extension.

The petitioner expressly challenged Notification No. 56/2023-CT (¶1), so the extension issue came up in this case. The court set aside the orders on the separate ground that they were unreasoned and kept the notification challenge open (¶5–7). The dates quoted from ¶2 do not, by themselves, prove NoticeCheck’s claim that the order was timely only under the extension.

The officer’s order says a personal hearing was scheduled for 28 June and another for 1 August 2024 (¶2). The taxpayer did not attend; the judgment does not find that no opportunity was offered. Nobody raised it as a separate ground before the court. The orders were quashed for lack of reasons (¶1, ¶5–6).
The officer used a stock phrase to dismiss the taxpayer’s reply (¶2). The court held that this showed non-application of mind and that the order was wholly unreasoned, then quashed it (¶1, ¶3–6).
The notice is described as covering April 2019 to March 2020, a single financial year (¶2). The court made no finding about notices spanning multiple financial years (¶1, ¶5–6).
The notice and order were under section 73, so a complaint about using section 74 without alleging fraud or suppression does not apply (¶2).

missed: The court’s finding that the officer rejected the reply without meaningful reasons or application of mind (¶1–5) is the defect NoticeCheck already flagged as a non-speaking order in #15. Its “no defect” answer to #20 was wrong, but it did not miss a separate court-found defect.

comment: NoticeCheck cited the wrong paragraph. The court said portal upload is legally sufficient service, but when repeated portal notices drew no response, the officer should have tried another section 169 mode. It found a lack of effective opportunity and set the orders aside subject to payment (¶7–10). The excerpt from ¶2 says nothing about service.

The cited passage gives the tax period and order dates, but no finding that a section 73 deadline was missed (head/¶0). The court addressed notice and the missing personal hearing, then set the orders aside on those grounds (¶3, ¶5, ¶7–10). It did not decide limitation.

It contains no section 168A challenge or finding about COVID extension notifications. he submissions and findings concern notice, personal hearing and remand (¶3–10). NoticeCheck’s further claim that extensions could not affect timeliness is not established by the dates in the head/¶0 alone.

The challenged assessment is identified as concerning 2020–21; the judgment gives no indication that one notice covered several financial years (head/¶0). The court’s findings address notice and hearing, not consolidation of years (¶3–10).
The challenged assessment order was under section 73, so this section 74 issue does not apply (head/¶0).

missed: No personal hearing was provided before the assessment order. The State’s counsel admitted this, and the court set the order aside and directed a hearing on remand (¶5, ¶7, ¶10(iii)).

comment: The cited passage shows that the order was issued in a deceased person’s name; it says nothing about whether the order gave reasons (¶2). The court framed the issue as whether notice and an order could be issued against the deceased proprietor (¶3, ¶6), and quashed them on that basis (¶7.9–8). Its direction to give a reasoned order in any future proceeding does not find the original order non-speaking (¶9.2).

Despite knowing the proprietor had died, the authority issued the SCN and order in his name (¶2, ¶7.3–7.4). The court held both legally unsustainable and quashed them; any new proceeding must be directed to the legal representative (¶7.9–9).

The cited reply was to a different SCN, and that proceeding was dropped (¶2.5). It does not show whether the reply in the challenged proceeding was considered; that separate proceeding is described in ¶2.6–2.7. The court framed and decided the case around the notice and order being issued in a deceased person’s name (¶3, ¶6, ¶7.9–8).

The cited notice is the first, separate proceeding, whose allegations were dropped (¶2.4–2.5). The judgment does not compare the demand in the challenged order with the demand or grounds in its SCN (¶2.6–2.8). The court decided the dead-person notice and order issue (¶3, ¶6, ¶7.9–8).

It gives the tax period and notice date, but does not assess the section 73 time limit (¶2). The cited order that dropped allegations belongs to a different proceeding (¶2.5). The court decided whether notice and an order could be issued in the deceased proprietor’s name, and left other grounds open for any new proceeding (¶3, ¶6, ¶7.9–9.2).

It contains no challenge to section 168A or a COVID extension notification. The court identified the sole issue as proceedings against the deceased proprietor (¶3, ¶6) and decided on that basis (¶7.9–8). NoticeCheck’s additional claim that extensions could not affect timeliness is not established by the judgment.
The challenged notice concerns FY 2021–22 only (¶2, ¶9). The judgment does not describe one notice covering multiple financial years. The court decided the deceased-proprietor issue (¶3, ¶6, ¶7.9–8).
The challenged notice and order were issued under section 73, so this section 74 issue does not apply (¶2–3, ¶8).

missed: The court’s finding was that the SCN and order were issued against a deceased person, which NoticeCheck flagged in #31 (¶3, ¶6, ¶7.9–8).

comment: The limitation issue in ¶2 concerns the appeal under section 107. The court set aside the show cause notice because its demand was much higher than the earlier DRC-01A demand (¶4–5). Neither ¶2 nor ¶5 mentions section 168A, COVID extension notifications, or a challenge to their validity. The court’s reason for setting aside the show cause notice was the unexplained increase in demand between DRC-01A and DRC-01 (¶4–5). The note’s claim that the order was timely only because of those notifications is not established by this judgment.
The judgment identifies only FY 2019–20 (¶2 and ¶5); it gives no indication that one notice covered several financial years. The court did not assess whether a notice consolidated multiple years.
